title: No. 50 — Periodical Appeals to the People Considered (Madison)
paragraphs: Some may argue that instead of OCCASIONAL appeals to the people, which are open to the objections raised against them, PERIODICAL appeals are the proper and adequate means of PREVENTING AND CORRECTING INFRACTIONS OF THE CONSTITUTION.

Note that in examining these expedients, I am limiting myself to their fitness for ENFORCING the Constitution—keeping the several departments of power within their proper bounds—without specifically considering them as provisions for ALTERING the Constitution itself. In this first view, appeals to the people at fixed periods appear to be nearly as unsuitable as appeals on particular occasions as they emerge. If the periods are separated by short intervals, the measures to be reviewed and corrected will be of recent date and will be connected with all the circumstances that tend to vitiate and pervert the result of occasional revisions. If the periods are far apart, the same remark will apply to all recent measures. And while the remoteness of the others may favor a dispassionate review of them, this advantage is inseparable from inconveniences that seem to counterbalance it. First, a distant prospect of public censure would be a very feeble restraint on power against those excesses to which it might be driven by the force of present motives. Is it to be imagined that a legislative assembly of one or two hundred members, eagerly bent on some favorite object and breaking through constitutional restraints in pursuit of it, would be stopped in its course by considerations drawn from a censorial review of their conduct ten, fifteen, or twenty years in the future? Second, the abuses would often have completed their harmful effects before the remedial provision could be applied. And finally, where this might not be the case, they would be of long standing, would have taken deep root, and would not easily be eradicated.

The scheme of revising the constitution to correct recent breaches of it, along with other purposes, has actually been tried in one of the States. One of the objects of the Council of Censors that met in Pennsylvania in 1783 and 1784 was, as we have seen, to inquire "whether the constitution had been violated, and whether the legislative and executive departments had encroached upon each other." This important and novel political experiment deserves very particular attention from several angles. In some respects, perhaps—as a single experiment made under somewhat peculiar circumstances—it may not be considered absolutely conclusive. But as applied to the case under consideration, it involves some facts that I venture to note as a complete and satisfactory illustration of the reasoning I have employed.

First. It appears, from the names of the gentlemen who composed the council, that some at least of its most active members had also been active and leading figures in the parties that already existed in the State.

Second. It appears that the same active and leading members of the council had been active and influential members of the legislative and executive branches within the period to be reviewed. They had even been patrons or opponents of the very measures now to be tested against the constitution. Two of the members had been vice-presidents of the State, and several others had served on the executive council within the seven preceding years. One of them had been speaker, and a number of others were distinguished members of the legislative assembly within the same period.

Third. Every page of their proceedings testifies to the effect of all these circumstances on the temper of their deliberations. Throughout the council's existence, it was split into two fixed and violent parties. The fact is acknowledged and lamented by the members themselves. Had that not been the case, the face of their proceedings supplies an equally satisfactory proof. On every question, however unimportant in itself or unconnected with the others, the same names stand invariably opposed on the rival columns. Any unbiased observer may infer, without danger of mistake and without meaning to reflect on either party or any individuals of either, that PASSION, not REASON, unfortunately must have presided over their decisions. When men exercise their reason coolly and freely on a variety of distinct questions, they inevitably fall into different opinions on some of them. When they are governed by a common passion, their opinions—if they can even be called opinions—will be the same.

Fourth. It is at least debatable whether the decisions of this body, in several instances, did not misconstrue the limits set for the legislative and executive departments instead of reducing and confining them to their constitutional places.

Fifth. I have never understood that the council's decisions on constitutional questions, whether rightly or wrongly formed, had any effect in changing the practice founded on legislative constructions. It even appears, if I am not mistaken, that in one instance the contemporary legislature denied the council's constructions and actually prevailed in the contest.
This censorial body therefore proves at the same time, by its investigations, the existence of the disease, and by its example, the ineffectiveness of the remedy.

This conclusion cannot be overturned by saying that the State in which the experiment was made was at that crisis, and had been for a long time before, violently heated and distracted by the rage of party. Is it to be presumed that at any future seven-year period the same State will be free from parties? Is it to be presumed that any other State, at the same or any other given period, will be exempt from them? Such an event ought to be neither presumed nor desired. The extinction of parties necessarily implies either a universal alarm for the public safety, or the absolute extinction of liberty.

Even if the precaution were taken of excluding from the assemblies elected by the people—those convened to review the previous administration of the government—all persons who had been involved with the government within that period, the difficulties would not be removed. The important task would probably fall on men who, having inferior capacities, would in other respects be little better qualified. Although they might not have been personally involved in the administration, and therefore not direct agents in the measures to be examined, they would probably have been entangled in the parties connected with those measures and have been elected under their auspices.
